An alternative would be to retain State authority for the taking of resident endangered species. This could have some disadvantages. Some States have not enacted endangered species legislation and some have not provided protection for all endangered species. Some may not be responsive ·to all endangered forms or populations within their borders, especially subspecies, and amphibians, reptiles, molluscs, and crustaceans. Endangered species are of national and not of just State significance. Unfavorable economic aspects of some endangered species could influence State governments to act contrary to the wishes of a broader segment of the public represented by the Federal Government. On the other hand it is argued that retaining State control maintains State incentives to carry out management practices, including protection, and that the Federal Government does not have the manpower to adequately handle resident endangered wildlife. It is pointed out the Federal Government must rely primarily on the States for endangered species field programs. Most States feel they are fully capable of handling resident endangered species management, including protection, and feel Federal preemption of their authority is unnecessary. They point to progress already made.
Alternative 4: A modification of alternative 3 would be to retain State authority for the taking of resident endangered species, but with the proviso that the Secretary would exercise regulatory authority when and where in his judgment a State had not developed a satisfactory program for species protection. It would place the Secretary in a position of being a "watch dog" but would lessen the impact of that part of the proposed legislation that the States feel is objectionable. There could be unfortunate delays in determining when a State did not have a satisfactory program.
